stem:
A 25-day-old term female infant is brought to your regional emergency department by her mother with 6 hours of a rectal temperature of 38.4 C at home. She has been feeding less well since this morning, taking about half her usual volume, and has had two wet nappies today rather than her usual five to six. There has been no cough, coryza, rash or diarrhoea. Delivery was normal vaginal at 39 weeks; the mother's group B streptococcus swab was negative and there was no prolonged rupture of membranes.

On arrival she is lying quietly in her mother's arms with a weak cry when handled and mild peripheral mottling. Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is no rash, no focal source on ear or throat examination, and the chest is clear to auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 72/44, RR 58, SpO2 97% on room air, temp 38.6 C axillary
data_table.Examination: Weak cry; peripheral mottling with capillary refill 3 seconds; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; no rash; ears and throat clear; chest clear; abdomen soft with no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 3.9 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.32 lactate 2.6 mmol/L; urinalysis clean-catch pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and a catheter urine specimen, then observe for 4 hours off antibiotics before deciding on lumbar puncture and empirical therapy
options.rationale: A febrile infant under 28 days is high-risk regardless of appearance and requires a full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics without waiting to see the trajectory. Observation windows apply to well-appearing infants over 60 days in some risk-tool pathways, not to neonates. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Obtain blood cultures, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate, and CSF by lumbar puncture, then give empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin without delay
options.rationale: RCH mandates a full septic workup with LP and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime) for any febrile infant under 1 month, particularly one who is unwell-appearing. Antibiotics must not be delayed beyond an hour by procedure attempts. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and urine by catheter, start empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, and defer lumbar puncture until the infant is more stable
options.rationale: The infant is haemodynamically stable enough to undergo LP alongside blood and urine sampling; deferring the LP means empirical treatment could not later be shortened based on CSF and risks missing meningitis. LP is only deferred in true haemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, or raised intracranial pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Obtain blood cultures, urine by catheter, and CSF by lumbar puncture, then give empirical IV ceftriaxone as monotherapy without additional agents
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone as monotherapy under 1 month is avoided in Australian paediatric practice because of bilirubin displacement and inadequate listeria cover; the RCH neonatal sepsis regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin). (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Perform a viral respiratory swab and urinalysis first and give empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin only if either result is positive for infection
options.rationale: In a febrile infant under 28 days a positive viral swab does not exclude serious bacterial infection and cannot defer antibiotics; the RCH pathway is empirical treatment for all, with de-escalation guided by cultures and CSF, not by viral testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: A febrile infant under 1 month is treated as high-risk for serious bacterial infection irrespective of appearance. RCH mandates a full septic workup (blood, urine by catheter or SPA, and CSF) alongside empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin without delay. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is inappropriate under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement and insufficient listeria cover. Deferring LP is reserved for true instability, coagulopathy, or raised intracranial pressure.
key_points: Under 28 days: full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics for any fever
First-line empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy is avoided under 1 month
Viral positive result does NOT rule out concurrent bacterial infection in this age
explanation.pearls: In a neonate with fever, blood cultures and empirical benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin should be delivered within the hour; procedure delays never justify pushing antibiotics past 60 minutes.

sources.label: eTG complete: Neonatal sepsis empirical therapy

stem:
A 22-month-old boy weighing 12 kg is brought to your paediatric emergency department with two days of watery diarrhoea, four episodes today of non-bilious vomiting, and reduced oral intake. His parents report he has had three small wet nappies in the last 12 hours and has been less playful than usual but is still recognising them. He has no significant past medical history and immunisations are up to date including rotavirus.

He has been offered oral rehydration solution in the waiting room over the last hour but has vomited each of the three attempts within minutes of drinking. He is tolerating small sips of water in between. There is no blood in the stool and no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/58, RR 30, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; mucous membranes dry; skin turgor mildly reduced; no acidotic breathing; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.36 base excess -3 mmol/L; urinalysis specific gravity 1.025

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert a peripheral intravenous cannula and give a 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 15 minutes
options.rationale: This child has mild to moderate dehydration without shock (warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert). RCH reserves rapid IV fluid bolus for severe dehydration or shock; earlier escalation adds cannulation morbidity without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Insert a peripheral intravenous cannula and commence a maintenance rate of 4-2-1 formula plus 5 percent deficit replacement in one third normal saline
options.rationale: IV maintenance-plus-deficit is used when the child is severely dehydrated or NGT rehydration has failed; RCH avoids IV as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration and one third normal saline is not the recommended paediatric maintenance fluid because of hyponatraemia risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give an oral single dose of ondansetron 4 milligrams and then re-attempt oral rehydration solution by mouth in small aliquots over one hour
options.rationale: Ondansetron helps break vomiting but the RCH ondansetron dose for a 12 kg child is 2 mg, not 4 mg (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg). Wrong-dose prescribing is the reason this distractor is unsafe here even though the pathway is right. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Admit for observation with sips of clear fluids only for the next four hours and reassess hydration before making a rehydration plan
options.rationale: Watchful observation without active rehydration prolongs deficit correction and risks progression; RCH escalates directly from failed oral to NGT within the ED assessment window rather than waiting hours to review. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and commence oral rehydration solution at 25 millilitres per kilogram per hour over the first four hours
options.rationale: RCH first-line rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral is nasogastric ORS, typically 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours or over the deficit period. NGT rehydration is non-inferior to IV, less resource-intense, and preserves gut function. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: This child has mild to moderate dehydration that failed the trial of oral rehydration. RCH pathway escalates to nasogastric ORS at approximately 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours before considering IV fluids. NGT rehydration is non-inferior to IV, less invasive, and preserves gut function. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure. Ondansetron may be a useful adjunct but the weight-banded dose is 2 mg for 8-15 kg, not 4 mg.
key_points: NGT ORS is first-line when oral fails and the child is mild-moderate dehydrated
IV fluids reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure
Ondansetron weight bands: 8-15 kg gets 2 mg, 15-30 kg gets 4 mg
Isotonic (0.9%) not third-normal saline is standard IV maintenance in AU paediatric practice
explanation.pearls: For a vomiting toddler with mild-moderate dehydration, an NGT delivering 25 mL/kg/hour of ORS beats jumping to a cannula; save the drip for shock or NGT failure.

stem:
A 2-year-old boy weighing 13 kg presents at 11 pm to your paediatric emergency department with a barking cough that started this evening. He was well earlier in the day with mild coryza for two days. He has a hoarse voice and audible stridor at rest that started 30 minutes ago. His mother reports he settled somewhat in the cool night air on the way in.

On examination he is alert and clinging to his mother. There is intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest with mild sternal recession, no cyanosis, and no drooling. He is speaking in short sentences and has a wet-sounding cough. There is no rash and no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 32, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 37.5 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; peripheries warm; capillary refill 2 seconds; inspiratory stridor at rest with mild sternal recession; no drooling; no cyanosis; chest clear other than transmitted upper airway noise
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate steroid regimen?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram as a single dose and observe for 3 hours before discharge planning
options.rationale: RCH recommends oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild to moderate croup and reserves 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with impending respiratory failure. Stridor at rest with mild recession fits the moderate band. Observation for 3 hours after last treatment is standard before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 milligrams per kilogram single dose and admit to the paediatric ward for overnight monitoring for 12 hours
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with marked recession, agitation, or hypoxia; using it here overdoses a moderate case without additional benefit and unnecessary admission adds cost. Discharge home after 3 hours of stability is appropriate for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 milligrams as a single dose delivered over 10 minutes and discharge home after 60 minutes of observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is second-line when oral dexamethasone is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred because it is systemic, well-absorbed, and cheaper. Sixty minutes is also too short an observation period for moderate croup with stridor at rest. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 milligram per kilogram single dose and observe for 3 hours before discharge to the community with follow-up
options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg has been used in some settings but has a shorter duration of action than dexamethasone and higher rates of representation. RCH lists dexamethasone as first-line and prednisolone as a fall-back if dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 solution first, then oral dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram single dose and 3 hour observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline in RCH pathway is reserved for severe croup or moderate croup deteriorating despite steroid, not for a first presentation of stable moderate croup at initial triage. Steroid alone is enough for stridor at rest without hypoxia or exhaustion. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: This is moderate croup (stridor at rest, mild recession, no exhaustion or hypoxia). RCH pathway is oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with 3 hours of observation before discharge. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with impending respiratory failure. Nebulised adrenaline is added only for severe croup or if moderate croup deteriorates despite steroid. Nebulised budesonide is a second-line steroid route.
key_points: 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone for mild to moderate croup
0.6 mg/kg oral dexamethasone reserved for severe croup
Observe 3 hours after last treatment before discharge
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose is escalation, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Use 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone only when respiratory failure is impending; the 0.15 mg/kg dose is the RCH default for stridor at rest without exhaustion.

stem:
A 20-month-old girl who had a routine antenatal 20 week morphology scan and follow-up 32 week scan both reporting normal kidneys and urinary tract presents to her general practitioner two weeks after completing a course of oral trimethoprim for a first culture-confirmed E coli urinary tract infection. She had a clean-catch urine sample that grew 100,000 CFU per mL of E coli fully sensitive to trimethoprim. She defervesced within 48 hours of starting antibiotics.

She is otherwise well, meeting developmental milestones, and has no palpable abdominal mass. Her growth trajectory is on the 50th centile and stable. Her mother has heard from a friend that her child should have a renal ultrasound and asks about imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 98/60, RR 24, SpO2 100% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no dysmorphism; abdomen soft with no palpable mass; genitalia normal; spine normal with no sacral dimple
data_table.Investigations: Follow-up urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites; renal function within normal limits from admission bloods

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: DMSA renal scan at 3 months post infection to exclude renal scarring and vesicoureteric reflux with subsequent decision on prophylactic antibiotics
options.rationale: DMSA is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI; it is a NICE construct with limited evidence for changing management. RCH follows a stepped ultrasound-then-consider-MCUG pathway only in atypical or recurrent presentations, not routinely. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks as she is under 24 months of age even though the UTI was typical E coli and antenatal scans were reassuring
options.rationale: This is the NICE construct of universal imaging in children under 24 months; the RCH cascade specifically states no routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI when antenatal monitoring was normal and response was rapid, even in children under 24 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No routine imaging required as she has had one typical UTI with documented antenatal renal tract monitoring and rapid response to first line antibiotics
options.rationale: RCH pathway does NOT recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a child over 6 months with documented antenatal renal tract monitoring and rapid clinical response. Ultrasound is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response after 48 hours, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram at 3 months post infection to exclude vesicoureteric reflux before deciding whether prophylactic antibiotics are indicated
options.rationale: MCUG is only considered in the RCH cascade after ultrasound shows an abnormality, in recurrent UTI, or in atypical presentations. It carries irradiation and catheterisation morbidity and is not routine after a typical first UTI with normal antenatal scans. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Contrast-enhanced renal MRI at 6 weeks to characterise renal parenchyma with a view to specialist renal outpatient review before repeat culture
options.rationale: MRI is not part of any Australian paediatric UTI pathway. It carries anaesthetic morbidity in a toddler with no benefit above ultrasound and is reserved for tertiary specialist-driven questions in structural or oncological cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: This child had a typical first UTI (E coli, rapid response, no red flags) with normal antenatal renal tract monitoring. RCH cascade does NOT recommend routine imaging in this scenario; ultrasound is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response after 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not part of the RCH cascade. This is a common exam trap where NICE-derived teaching contradicts the local Australian pathway.
key_points: RCH: no routine imaging after single typical UTI with normal antenatal scans
US indicated for atypical UTI or recurrent UTI (not routine)
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not in the RCH cascade
Atypical criteria: poor response 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, mass, raised creatinine
explanation.pearls: When a first UTI is E coli, rapid to respond, and follows normal antenatal scans, RCH stops at reassurance; NICE would over-image. Cite RCH to justify no imaging.

stem:
A 6-week-old former term male infant is admitted overnight in July with moderate bronchiolitis. He has been on nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute for the last 2 hours 15 minutes to maintain SpO2 above 90 percent. Immediately before the trial, his SpO2 was 88 percent in room air. Feeds have been paused because he is working too hard to feed.

On the third hourly review he still has moderate subcostal and intercostal recession with fine crackles throughout. His SpO2 is now 90 percent on 1 L per minute nasal prongs but he has had two brief apnoeic episodes in the last hour that resolved with mild stimulation. He is drowsier than at admission but rousable and pink.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 76/48, RR 68, SpO2 90% on 1 L/min nasal prong oxygen, temp 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; moderate subcostal and intercostal recession; nasal flare; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; bilateral fine crackles with wheeze; two brief apnoeic episodes in the last hour resolving with stimulation
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.30 pCO2 55 mmHg bicarbonate 27 mmol/L base excess 0 mmol/L; NPA positive for RSV; chest x-ray hyperinflation without focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 2 litres per minute and reassess in another 2 hours with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring in place
options.rationale: Persistence of increased work of breathing plus recurrent apnoea after a full low-flow trial meets RCH criteria for escalation; continuing low-flow risks further deterioration. Low-flow above 2 L/min is also not standard because gas mixing is unreliable. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline 3 percent nebulised 4 millilitres and continue current low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute with 2 hourly review
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway and its evidence base is weak. It does not address hypoxia, recurrent apnoea, or CO2 retention. (Source: PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline 2022)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 0.5 milligrams via 6 litres per minute driving oxygen every 20 minutes for 3 doses and reassess work of breathing
options.rationale: Salbutamol has consistently failed to alter the natural history of bronchiolitis in infants and is not recommended by RCH in this age group. Escalating to a bronchodilator in a hypercapnic, apnoeic infant delays effective respiratory support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence bubble continuous positive airway pressure at 5 centimetres of water via mask and defer PICU discussion until this fails
options.rationale: Bubble CPAP via mask in a young infant with recurrent apnoea is escalation beyond ward capability and requires PICU input in parallel, not deferred. RCH pathway favours HFNC as the intermediate step before CPAP or intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 90 percent and PICU liaison for potential transfer
options.rationale: RCH permits HFNC after documented failure of low-flow (2 hours) with persistent hypoxia, marked work of breathing, or recurrent apnoea. Dose is 2 L/kg/min in this weight bracket, titrated to the same 90 percent SpO2 target. Apnoea plus rising pCO2 mandates PICU liaison. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This infant has failed a 2 hour trial of low-flow nasal prong oxygen with persistent hypoxia, marked work of breathing, recurrent apnoea, and rising pCO2. RCH permits escalation to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min in this weight bracket, still titrating to SpO2 90 percent. Apnoea plus hypercapnia mandates PICU liaison in parallel to escalation. Salbutamol has no role in bronchiolitis under 12 months. CPAP is a further escalation beyond HFNC and hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH pathway.
key_points: Low-flow trial for 2 hours is prerequisite before HFNC escalation
HFNC dose in this weight is 2 L/kg/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent
Recurrent apnoea plus rising pCO2 triggers PICU liaison
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway
explanation.pearls: Recurrent apnoea in RSV bronchiolitis under 3 months plus hypercapnia is your PICU-call trigger; escalate to HFNC while making the call, do not wait for the transfer team to arrive.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 10 minutes after eating a cashew biscuit at a birthday party. He has a known peanut allergy but has not previously reacted to tree nuts. He developed generalised urticaria within 5 minutes and now has audible wheeze, hoarse voice, and a swollen tongue.

On arrival he is anxious with generalised urticaria, marked lip and periorbital swelling, biphasic stridor, and audible wheeze. He speaks in short phrases. There is no cyanosis and pulses are palpable. IV access has not yet been obtained. There is no known cardiac history and he has never used an adrenaline autoinjector.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 78/44, RR 40, SpO2 93% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Anxious; generalised urticaria; periorbital and lip swelling; biphasic stridor; audible expiratory wheeze; speaking in short phrases; capillary refill 3 seconds; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms of 1:1000 to the anterolateral thigh with cardiac monitoring throughout and preparation to repeat
options.rationale: The 150 microgram dose covers the 10-20 kg band; this child at 18 kg sits at the top of that band with severe features, but the ASCIA banded table in the 20+ kg space would be 300 mcg. RCH aligns with ASCIA using 150 mcg for 10-20 kg and 300 mcg for over 20 kg. Note this child weighs 18 kg so 150 mcg is technically correct for the band but option B tests whether the candidate reaches for weight-based arithmetic. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline calculated at 10 micrograms per kilogram giving 180 micrograms of 1:1000 to the anterolateral thigh with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Weight-based 10 mcg/kg calculation is not the ASCIA or RCH first-line pathway in a school-age paediatric anaphylaxis. Banded IM dosing avoids maths errors under pressure and is the AU standard. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms of 1:1000 to the anterolateral thigh with cardiac monitoring throughout and prepare to repeat every 5 minutes
options.rationale: This child weighs 18 kg (10-20 kg band = 150 mcg) but severity plus wheeze and stridor mandate escalation; some hospital algorithms use 300 mcg for children approaching 20 kg with severe airway involvement. In practice the ASCIA table shifts to 300 mcg at 20 kg and above; several AU EDs allow rounding upward at high-band weight with severe features. The intent of the question is testing the banded ASCIA approach over kg-based arithmetic. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms of 1:10000 as an initial bolus after IV access with cardiac monitoring and repeated titration to response
options.rationale: IV adrenaline in paediatric anaphylaxis is reserved for refractory shock after two IM doses; jumping to IV first risks arrhythmia and delays effective early IM treatment during airway compromise. IM is first-line even when IV access will be needed later. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 with high flow oxygen and 200 milligrams of hydrocortisone as first-line pharmacotherapy while awaiting IV access
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptoms but is not a substitute for IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis, which acts systemically. Steroids do not treat the acute reaction and are second-line. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is severe paediatric anaphylaxis with airway compromise. ASCIA and RCH advise IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh using a banded dose table rather than weight-based arithmetic to avoid dosing errors under pressure. The 10-20 kg band is 150 mcg (EpiPen Jr equivalent) and the 20+ kg band is 300 mcg (EpiPen). At 18 kg with severe airway features, several AU EDs allow rounding to the 300 mcg dose to reflect the severity and proximity to the 20 kg cutoff. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory shock and nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway symptoms but does not replace IM.
key_points: ASCIA banded IM adrenaline: 10-20 kg is 150 mcg; over 20 kg is 300 mcg
IM anterolateral thigh route first-line; repeat every 5 min
IV adrenaline only after 2 IM doses fail (refractory shock)
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts not first-line for anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: Do not calculate adrenaline in mg/kg during a paediatric anaphylaxis; grab the ASCIA band and give 150 mcg or 300 mcg IM into the thigh without pausing to do sums.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl weighing 14 kg presents to a regional emergency department with 24 hours of fever to 40 C, poor feeding, and vomiting. She has been progressively drowsy since arrival. IV access was obtained on the second attempt, blood cultures drawn, and IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg given within 30 minutes of arrival. She then received a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 10 minutes.

Twenty minutes after completion of the first bolus she remains drowsy with cool peripheries and a mottled trunk. Her mucous membranes are dry and she has no purpuric rash. Her lactate has fallen from 5.2 to 4.4 mmol/L but her mean arterial pressure remains at 45 mmHg with a capillary refill of 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 78/52 (MAP 45), RR 34, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temp 39.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool mottled peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; no purpuric rash; abdomen soft; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.24 lactate 4.4 mmol/L base excess -8 mmol/L; sodium 138 potassium 4.2 creatinine 62 mmol/L; INR 1.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 10 minutes then reassess perfusion and lactate before considering inotropes
options.rationale: RCH paediatric sepsis pathway is up to 60 mL/kg in 20 mL/kg boluses in the first hour if perfusion remains inadequate, with inotropes triggered by ongoing shock after fluid or by signs of fluid overload. This child has residual shock with cool peripheries and a falling but still elevated lactate; a second bolus is warranted before inotropes. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Commence peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per minute now and defer further crystalloid until inotropes are running
options.rationale: Inotropes are triggered by fluid-refractory shock or by fluid-intolerant shock (rales, hepatomegaly, rising oxygen requirement) not by residual shock at 20 mL/kg. Skipping the second bolus is over-escalation and misses the RCH order (fluids first, up to 60 mL/kg, then inotropes). (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram albumin 4 percent bolus over 15 minutes now rather than a second crystalloid bolus to expand intravascular volume
options.rationale: RCH first-line fluid is isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or Hartmann's); albumin is not first-line and is reserved for specific indications after several crystalloid boluses. Choosing albumin now deviates from the AU pathway without evidence of benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 2 milligrams per kilogram now for possible adrenal insufficiency before proceeding with any further fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone in paediatric septic shock is considered after inotrope-refractory shock, not as an early step. Giving it before completing fluid resuscitation delays effective early treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Intubate for airway protection with cuffed tube and ketamine plus rocuronium induction before further fluid resuscitation is undertaken
options.rationale: This child is drowsy but rousable, maintaining airway, and oxygenating on Hudson mask; intubating during unresolved shock without preparatory fluid is risky (cardiovascular collapse on induction). Fluid resuscitate first, intubate if shock persists after full fluid and inotrope escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: This child has persistent septic shock after the first 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. The RCH pathway allows up to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid in 20 mL/kg boluses within the first hour before triggering inotropes, provided there are no signs of fluid-intolerant shock (rales, hepatomegaly, rising oxygen). Inotropes are for fluid-refractory or fluid-intolerant shock. Albumin, hydrocortisone, and early intubation are all later steps.
key_points: Up to 60 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour for paediatric septic shock
Inotropes trigger on fluid-refractory or fluid-intolerant shock
Isotonic crystalloid first-line; albumin second-line
Hydrocortisone is for inotrope-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: In septic shock at 20 mL/kg with residual mottling and lactate still above 4, the next move is another 20 mL/kg bolus; save adrenaline for after the full 60 mL/kg unless fluid intolerance emerges.

stem:
A 10-year-old girl weighing 30 kg presents to your paediatric emergency department with 2 days of polyuria, polydipsia, and progressive drowsiness. There is no known past history of diabetes. She was found by her father this morning slumped in bed and rousable only to voice.

On arrival she is drowsy with deep sighing respiration and a fruity odour on her breath. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. Her airway is patent and she is protecting it. She has no focal neurology and no signs of raised intracranial pressure. She is now on the ED trolley with IV access secured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 88/54 (MAP 65), RR 32 deep, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable (GCS 12); Kussmaul breathing; cool peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft; no focal neurology; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 32 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.05 bicarbonate 6 mmol/L base excess -22; ketones 5.6 mmol/L; sodium 128 potassium 5.4 chloride 96 corrected sodium 132; urinalysis ketones 4+ glucose 4+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?

options.text: Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 15 minutes then commence maintenance plus deficit calculated over 48 hours with an insulin infusion at 0.05 units per kilogram per hour after 1 hour of fluid
options.rationale: The 20 mL/kg bolus is only used in true shock (systolic BP <5th centile for age, unrecordable pulses); this child has poor perfusion but a MAP within acceptable range for age. The APEG and RCH pathway uses 10 mL/kg over 30-60 minutes for the initial bolus in DKA to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Insert nasogastric tube for gastric decompression then commence isotonic saline maintenance without a bolus and start subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogue every 4 hours
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin is not adequate for correcting DKA in this age; IV insulin infusion is standard. Delaying any bolus is inappropriate given poor perfusion, and gastric decompression alone does not address the acidosis. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 milliequivalent per kilogram over 1 hour and commence insulin infusion immediately at 0.1 units per kilogram per hour to reverse the ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening acidosis (pH <6.9) with cardiac depression, because it worsens paradoxical CSF acidosis and cerebral oedema. Immediate insulin without fluid loading also increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram Hartmann's solution bolus over 15 minutes then commence Plasma-Lyte 148 maintenance plus deficit over 24 hours with insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kilogram per hour from the outset
options.rationale: Deficit replacement over 24 hours is faster than the APEG/RCH-recommended 48 hours and increases cerebral oedema risk; the initial bolus is also 10 mL/kg not 20 mL/kg unless truly shocked. Immediate insulin is again unsafe. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Give a 10 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes then commence maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours with insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units per kilogram per hour
options.rationale: APEG and RCH DKA pathway uses a conservative 10 mL/kg bolus over 30-60 min to lower cerebral oedema risk, with rehydration over 48 hours at an assumed 7 percent deficit (moderate DKA) minus the bolus, plus maintenance. Insulin is delayed by 1 hour after starting fluid and started at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr. (Source: APEG/RCH: Paediatric DKA)

explanation.summary: This is moderate paediatric DKA with poor perfusion but not overt shock. APEG and RCH advise a conservative 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30-60 minutes (only 20 mL/kg if truly shocked with unrecordable pulses), then rehydration over 48 hours at an assumed 7 percent deficit minus the bolus, plus maintenance. Insulin infusion is started 1 hour after fluid at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr. Cerebral oedema is the feared complication and drives the conservative fluid approach. Bicarbonate is contraindicated except in life-threatening acidosis.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg in paediatric DKA (20 mL/kg only in true shock)
Rehydrate over 48 hours (not 24) to minimise cerebral oedema risk
Insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr, started 1 hour after fluid
Bicarbonate contraindicated except in pH <6.9 with cardiac depression
explanation.pearls: Do NOT rehydrate paediatric DKA over 24 hours; the APEG 48-hour deficit plus 10 mL/kg bolus schedule exists specifically to reduce cerebral oedema mortality.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki diagnosis and treatment window
stem:
A 5-month-old male infant presents to your regional paediatric ward on day 8 of fever to 39 C. He has had irritability, a fine erythematous rash on the trunk that came and went, and mild coryza. Empirical amoxicillin was started at day 3 by his general practitioner without effect. He was seen at day 5 in your ED and a septic screen including blood cultures was negative, and he was discharged home with reassurance.

He has been reviewed today by the paediatric registrar. He now has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, redness of the lips with cracking, and mild peripheral extremity swelling. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His mother reports his fingertips have started peeling this morning. He continues to have daily fevers.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, BP 88/52, RR 40, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate; erythematous cracked lips without ulceration; mild non-pitting oedema of the hands; fine peeling of fingertips; no cervical lymphadenopathy; no gallop or murmur; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 18 x10^9/L; platelets 620 x10^9/L; C-reactive protein 145 mg/L; ESR 78 mm/hr; alanine transaminase 92 U/L; albumin 28 g/L; urinalysis 30 white cells per high power field with no organisms; echocardiogram shows a right coronary artery Z score of 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 grams per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 milligrams per kilogram per day and arrange formal cardiology review
options.rationale: This is incomplete (atypical) Kawasaki disease: fever more than 5 days plus 2 principal criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes) with supportive laboratory features (raised platelets, ALT, low albumin, sterile pyuria, raised CRP/ESR) and a coronary artery Z score more than 2. IVIG 2 g/kg is indicated within 10 days of fever onset to lower coronary aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent, together with aspirin. Coronary Z score 2.6 also independently supports treatment. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

options.text: Await repeat inflammatory markers in 48 hours before treating with intravenous immunoglobulin as he does not meet the 4 of 5 principal criteria for complete Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: The incomplete Kawasaki algorithm mandates immediate treatment when fever more than 5 days plus supportive labs plus coronary changes are present, even without 4 of 5 principal criteria. Delaying past day 10 substantially raises aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 milligrams per kilogram daily for 3 days as first-line treatment while withholding intravenous immunoglobulin because of infection risk
options.rationale: First-line treatment is IVIG plus aspirin. Steroids are added upfront only in Kobayashi-high-risk patients (Japanese scoring) or as adjuncts, not as monotherapy. Withholding IVIG delays effective aneurysm prevention. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 milligrams per kilogram daily and vancomycin pending repeat blood cultures given persistent fever and irritability
options.rationale: There is no infectious source and the clinical picture, laboratory profile, and coronary changes point to Kawasaki disease; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics would delay IVIG and are not appropriate. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe oral aspirin 30 milligrams per kilogram per day monotherapy and reassess with echocardiogram in 6 weeks before deciding on intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Aspirin alone does not reduce aneurysm risk; IVIG is the aneurysm-preventing agent. Deferring for 6 weeks is well past the IVIG treatment window and would result in preventable coronary damage. (Source: AHA/RANZCPCH Kawasaki disease guidelines)

explanation.summary: This child on day 8 of fever meets the incomplete Kawasaki disease algorithm: fever more than 5 days, 2 principal criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes), supportive laboratory features (platelets 620, ALT 92, albumin 28, CRP 145, sterile pyuria), and a coronary Z score of 2.6. Immediate IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is indicated within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. Steroid monotherapy, ongoing antibiotics, or aspirin monotherapy are all inappropriate.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever more than 5 days plus supportive labs plus coronary Z more than 2
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is first-line and should be given within 10 days of fever onset
Coronary Z score more than 2 alone justifies treatment
Delaying past day 10 increases aneurysm risk substantially
explanation.pearls: Do not wait for the 4th and 5th principal Kawasaki criteria in an infant; incomplete Kawasaki with any coronary Z more than 2 or supportive lab profile gets IVIG within the 10-day window.

stem:
A 12-day-old female infant delivered at 36 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean is admitted to your regional special care nursery with 8 hours of poor feeding, lethargy, and one episode of a brief focal right-sided upper limb clonic movement lasting 30 seconds. She had been feeding well at home since discharge on day 4. The mother was group B streptococcus positive and received one dose of intrapartum benzylpenicillin 4 hours before delivery.

On arrival the infant is lethargic with a bulging anterior fontanelle and increased tone. Her cardiovascular examination is unremarkable with capillary refill 2 seconds and warm peripheries. Blood cultures and CSF have been drawn. Head ultrasound at the bedside shows echogenicity in the periventricular white matter but no hydrocephalus or established parenchymal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, BP 68/40, RR 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 38.4 C axillary
data_table.Examination: Lethargic; anterior fontanelle bulging; tone increased in all four limbs; no rash; abdomen soft with liver 2 cm below costal margin; peripheries warm; brief focal right upper limb clonic movement witnessed
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 24 x10^9/L neutrophils 15; CRP 88 mg/L; venous gas pH 7.34 lactate 3.1 mmol/L; blood glucose 3.8 mmol/L; CSF opening pressure not measured, WBC 480 per microlitre (85 percent polymorphs), protein 2.1 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L (paired serum 4.8), Gram stain pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin at the standard neonatal doses without additional agents pending culture results
options.rationale: For late-onset neonatal sepsis (over 48 hours) with meningitis and confirmed CSF pleocytosis, cover must extend to meningitic doses of a cephalosporin because CNS penetration of gentamicin is limited. Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the empirical early-onset (under 48 hours) neonatal sepsis regimen, not late-onset with meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime at meningitic dosing plus benzylpenicillin plus aciclovir intravenous at 20 milligrams per kilogram three times daily
options.rationale: Late-onset neonatal sepsis with meningitis in a 12-day-old requires meningitic-dose cefotaxime (for GBS, E coli, other Gram negatives) plus benzylpenicillin (adds listeria cover) plus IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8 hourly for empirical HSV encephalitis cover given seizure activity. Ceftriaxone is avoided under 1 month for bilirubin displacement reasons; cefotaxime is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone at 100 milligrams per kilogram daily plus vancomycin at 15 milligrams per kilogram every 6 hours as the primary empirical regimen
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement and hypocalcaemia risk; cefotaxime is preferred. Vancomycin is added if there is suspicion of coagulase-negative staphylococcus (indwelling lines) which is not obvious here. HSV cover is also missing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin plus gentamicin plus a single dose of intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin does not cover GBS, listeria, or Gram-negative meningitis adequately in this age. Dexamethasone before antibiotics is a paediatric bacterial meningitis (over 2 months) intervention and its role in neonatal meningitis is unproven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 40 milligrams per kilogram every 8 hours as monotherapy empirically pending sensitivity results and cerebrospinal fluid PCR
options.rationale: Meropenem monotherapy is not first-line empirical treatment for community-onset late-onset neonatal sepsis with meningitis; it is reserved for resistant Gram-negative sepsis or ESBL exposure. HSV cover is still needed given the seizure activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Neonatal sepsis)

explanation.summary: Late-onset (over 48 hours) neonatal sepsis with meningitis and seizure activity in a 12-day-old requires empirical cover for GBS, E coli, other Gram negatives, listeria (still possible in the first month), and HSV. The standard AU empirical regimen is meningitic-dose IV cefotaxime (avoiding ceftriaxone under 1 month), plus IV benzylpenicillin (listeria), plus IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8 hourly (HSV encephalitis). Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin alone is the early-onset neonatal sepsis regimen and does not have adequate CNS penetration.
key_points: Late-onset neonatal meningitis: IV cefotaxime meningitic dose plus benzylpenicillin plus aciclovir
Ceftriaxone avoided under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement
Aciclovir empirical cover for HSV when neonatal seizures present
Early-onset regimen (benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin) is inadequate for late-onset meningitis
explanation.pearls: In a 12-day-old with seizures and CSF pleocytosis, add IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8-hourly to cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin without waiting for HSV PCR; the treatment window for HSV encephalitis is measured in hours.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate loading in renal impairment
stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents to your tertiary obstetric emergency department with a 4 hour history of frontal headache, epigastric pain, and one episode of visual flashing lights. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 and she had previously been well. She has no history of chronic kidney disease.

On arrival she is anxious with brisk reflexes and 3 beats of clonus at the ankles bilaterally. Uterus is soft with regular fetal movements felt by the mother. Cardiotocograph shows a normal reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. You have decided to commence magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and initiated antihypertensive treatment. IV access has been secured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 168/112, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; brisk reflexes with 3 beats of clonus; abdomen soft with fundal height 34 cm; no epigastric tenderness on palpation; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol; sodium 132 potassium 4.6 urea 8.2 creatinine 128 micromol/L; ALT 84 AST 78 platelets 118 x10^9/L; INR 1.1; uric acid 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 1 gram per hour with 4 hourly deep tendon reflex and urine output monitoring
options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends 4 g IV loading over 15-20 min then 1 g/hr maintenance for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia, with a reduced maintenance rate (1 g/hr rather than 2 g/hr) when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L. Deep tendon reflex loss and urine output under 100 mL over 4 hours trigger withholding. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 2 grams per hour with hourly reflex and urine output monitoring
options.rationale: The standard maintenance dose is 2 g/hr but this must be halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L to avoid toxic accumulation because magnesium is renally excreted. This patient has creatinine 128 micromol/L. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 6 grams intramuscularly plus 5 grams into each buttock with subsequent 5 grams intramuscularly every 4 hours per the Pritchard regimen
options.rationale: The Pritchard IM regimen is a historical alternative used where IV pumps are unavailable. In an AU tertiary setting the IV loading-plus-infusion regimen is standard because it allows real-time titration and monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Phenytoin loading 15 milligrams per kilogram intravenously over 30 minutes followed by 100 milligrams every 8 hours as an alternative anticonvulsant
options.rationale: Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate for eclampsia seizure prevention (Magpie and Collaborative Eclampsia Trial) and is no longer used as first-line. Magnesium is the SOMANZ standard. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Diazepam 10 milligrams intravenously over 2 minutes with observation for further seizures before considering magnesium sulfate infusion
options.rationale: Diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures unresponsive to magnesium; withholding magnesium in favour of diazepam prophylaxis is inappropriate and increases eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is severe pre-eclampsia with proteinuria, raised transaminases, thrombocytopenia, and neurological symptoms. SOMANZ recommends IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis at 4 g loading over 15-20 minutes followed by 2 g/hr maintenance, halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L because magnesium is renally cleared. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output. IM Pritchard regimen is a historical alternative and diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures.
key_points: SOMANZ MgSO4: 4 g load over 15-20 min then 1-2 g/hr maintenance
Halve maintenance to 1 g/hr when creatinine >100 micromol/L
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output for toxicity
Phenytoin and diazepam are not first-line for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: When creatinine rises above 100 micromol/L in severe pre-eclampsia, halve the magnesium maintenance to 1 g/hr; the loading dose stays 4 g.

RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

stem:
A 32-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 has just had an unassisted spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3800 gram baby after a labour of 14 hours. The third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units at delivery of the anterior shoulder. She has a booking blood pressure of 165/105, was diagnosed with chronic hypertension pre-pregnancy on labetalol, and has had blood pressures ranging 150-170 systolic through labour.

Within 5 minutes of placental delivery she has 900 mL of visible fresh red blood loss and the uterus feels soft on abdominal palpation. Vaginal examination reveals a bulky uterus with clots at the introitus and no vaginal or cervical tear identified. She has good IV access and the postpartum haemorrhage protocol has been activated with fluids running.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/62, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; uterus above the umbilicus and soft; no vaginal or cervical tear on inspection; no perineal haematoma
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 900 mL and ongoing; venous gas pH 7.36 haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128); coags awaited

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Intravenous ergometrine 250 micrograms as a slow push with cardiac monitoring in place and full uterotonic protocol continued
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes profound vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum blood pressures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intramuscular Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 international units and ergometrine 500 micrograms) with cardiac monitoring and continue full uterotonic protocol
options.rationale: Syntometrine contains ergometrine which is contraindicated in hypertension; giving it here risks hypertensive crisis and cerebrovascular accident. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units every 5 minutes up to 4 doses before escalation to any additional uterotonic
options.rationale: Repeat IM oxytocin doses without escalation to second-line uterotonics wastes time in an ongoing PPH; RANZCOG pathway is to start an oxytocin infusion (40 units in 1 L saline over 4 hours) then move to ergometrine or carboprost. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms plus intravenous tranexamic acid 1 gram over 10 minutes as combined pharmacotherapy before repeat oxytocin
options.rationale: Misoprostol 800 mcg (rectal or sublingual) is a fallback where injectable uterotonics are unavailable and is slower in onset; carboprost is preferred when it is available. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with bronchospasm precautions in place and repeat every 15 minutes up to 8 doses if bleeding continues
options.rationale: After oxytocin failure and where ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension, carboprost 250 mcg IM (Hemabate, F2-alpha prostaglandin) is the next-line uterotonic per RANZCOG PPH guidance. Bronchospasm precautions are needed. Doses may be repeated up to 8 total. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: This is a primary postpartum haemorrhage with atony after oxytocin. The RANZCOG uterotonic ladder is oxytocin (bolus then infusion), then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol. Ergometrine is CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension because of vasoconstriction and risk of hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum BP, so ergometrine (and Syntometrine which contains it) must be avoided; carboprost IM is the appropriate next-line uterotonic. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine (and Syntometrine) contraindicated in hypertension
Carboprost 250 mcg IM with bronchospasm precautions is next-line when ergometrine is contraindicated
TXA should be given but is haemostatic not uterotonic
explanation.pearls: In a PPH with chronic hypertension, skip ergometrine and go straight to carboprost; watch for bronchospasm in asthmatics.

subtopic_detail: Acute severe hypertension threshold and agent
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 30 plus 4 weeks with a known singleton pregnancy presents to your birth suite with a 3 hour history of persistent occipital headache. Booking blood pressure was 118/74 and she has been well since. She has no known drug allergies. She has been fasted for 6 hours in preparation for antenatal review.

On arrival to the birth suite the initial BP is 172/116, confirmed 15 minutes later at 168/114 with an appropriate cuff on the right arm. She is alert with no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, and no shortness of breath. Reflexes are 2+ without clonus. Bedside urinalysis shows protein 2+. Cardiotocograph shows a reactive trace with baseline 140 and moderate variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 168/114, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.7 C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Alert; reflexes 2+; no clonus; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles; abdomen soft with fundal height 30 cm and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis protein 2+; urine protein:creatinine ratio pending; sodium 138 potassium 4.4 urea 4.2 creatinine 74; ALT 32 platelets 220 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line agent to lower blood pressure?

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside titrated infusion at 0.3 micrograms per kilogram per minute with continuous arterial line monitoring for BP control
options.rationale: Nitroprusside is generally avoided in pregnancy because of cyanide accumulation risk in the fetus and requires ICU-level monitoring; it is reserved for refractory hypertensive emergency after other agents have failed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 milligrams to achieve rapid drop with cardiotocograph continuous throughout for fetal wellbeing monitoring
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is not recommended in pregnancy because uncontrolled rapid drops can cause fetal distress from placental hypoperfusion. Oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine at controlled doses are the SOMANZ options. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams as a slow push to reduce blood pressure and preload with careful reassessment of BP after 20 minutes
options.rationale: Furosemide is not a first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; it may worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia (which has capillary leak) and is reserved for pulmonary oedema. It does not treat the hypertension itself. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 milligrams and repeat blood pressure in 30 minutes with a second dose if systolic remains at or above 160
options.rationale: SOMANZ acute severe hypertension in pregnancy pathway lists oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate release (repeatable at 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg) as a first-line option alongside IV labetalol and IV hydralazine when BP is at least 160/110. Oral nifedipine is preferred when IV access is not needed for other reasons. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Oral captopril 25 milligrams as first-line antihypertensive with a target of achieving a systolic below 140 within one hour of administration
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and cause foetal renal dysgenesis; they are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Captopril is not appropriate at any dose antenatally. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at least 160/110 on two readings 15 minutes apart) with likely new-onset pre-eclampsia (proteinuria). SOMANZ first-line agents for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy are oral nifedipine immediate release, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, all in stepped protocols. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided (risk of uncontrolled fetal distress), nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases, and ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated. Furosemide is not an antihypertensive in this setting.
key_points: SOMANZ severe HTN threshold: 160/110 on two readings 15 min apart
First-line options: oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, IV hydralazine
ACE inhibitors absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic)
Sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside avoided
explanation.pearls: For severe HTN in pregnancy at 160/110, oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release is a legitimate first move when IV access is not otherwise needed; sublingual is not the same drug in a different route.

RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy surgical option with contralateral history
stem:
A 32-year-old gravida 4 para 1 presents to your gynaecology emergency assessment unit at 6 plus 5 weeks by dates with 6 hours of left iliac fossa pain and moderate vaginal spotting. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy. She has been trying to conceive since and has undergone no assisted reproductive therapy.

She is haemodynamically stable with mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation without peritonism. Speculum examination shows a small amount of dark blood at the cervical os. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with a yolk sac but no foetal cardiac activity, and 40 mL of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She strongly wishes to preserve future fertility.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation with no peritonism; abdomen otherwise soft; speculum shows small amount of dark blood at os; bimanual with left adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 4200 IU/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; blood group A rhesus positive; venous gas pH 7.40 lactate 1.4 mmol/L; transvaginal ultrasound as described above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingostomy with removal of ectopic tissue and preservation of the left fallopian tube for potential future spontaneous conception
options.rationale: Although salpingostomy classically preserves fertility, this patient has a prior contralateral salpingectomy meaning the left tube is her only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube is 15-30 percent, so leaving a damaged tube in place risks a further ectopic in the only remaining tube. RANZCOG accepts salpingectomy in this situation to lower recurrence risk, with IVF as the future fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 milligrams per square metre single dose with weekly beta-hCG follow-up until confirmed less than 15 international units per litre
options.rationale: This ectopic has yolk sac (though no cardiac activity) and moderate free fluid; RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate require beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L (met), mass under 3.5 cm (met), no significant pain, no haemorrhage, and no fetal cardiac activity. Moderate free fluid and worsening pain move her outside methotrexate territory. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with removal of ectopic tissue and the left fallopian tube with counselling that future fertility will require in vitro fertilisation
options.rationale: The T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy means the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube (15-30 percent) after salpingostomy dominates the fertility calculus in this scenario; salpingectomy plus IVF has a better cumulative live birth outcome than salpingostomy with a high recurrence chance. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy in this specific scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Expectant management with 48 hour beta-hCG monitoring and clinic review in one week without surgical or medical intervention at this stage
options.rationale: Expectant management is only appropriate for asymptomatic patients with declining beta-hCG under 1000-2000 IU/L, minimal free fluid, and no adnexal mass. This patient has a 2.8 cm mass with yolk sac, moderate free fluid, and pain. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Laparotomy through a Pfannenstiel incision with left salpingectomy and inspection of the contralateral surgical site for adhesions
options.rationale: Laparotomy is unnecessary in a haemodynamically stable patient with an unruptured tubal ectopic; laparoscopy has lower morbidity, shorter recovery, and comparable outcomes. Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or extensive adhesions preventing laparoscopy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: This is the T14 historical-bilaterality flip: normally salpingostomy is chosen over salpingectomy to preserve fertility, but when the contralateral tube has already been removed the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent, which dominates the fertility calculus. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy plus IVF as the higher cumulative live birth pathway in this specific scenario. Methotrexate is excluded by the moderate free fluid and yolk sac features, and expectant management is excluded by the mass and pain.
key_points: T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy makes salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy
Recurrent ectopic risk in same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent
Methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage
Laparotomy reserved for haemodynamic instability
explanation.pearls: In an ectopic patient with prior contralateral salpingectomy, do NOT try to preserve the only remaining tube; take it and offer IVF, because a repeat same-tube ectopic can end that tube anyway.

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR sequence after failed McRoberts
stem:
A 33-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 with a booking BMI of 34 and diet-controlled gestational diabetes is delivering at 39 plus 5 weeks. She has just delivered the fetal head after a normal first stage and 45 minutes of active second stage. The head has retracted tightly against the perineum (turtle sign) and gentle downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. She is in the lithotomy position with an epidural.

The accoucheur has called for help and the emergency buzzer has been pressed. The clock has been started. McRoberts hyperflexion of the hips has been performed by two assistants for 30 seconds without effect, then combined with suprapubic pressure applied by the second assistant from the anterior shoulder side for a further 30 seconds, also without effect. The head has now been undelivered for 90 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air; fetal HR 100 with reduced variability
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign present; anterior shoulder impacted behind the pubic symphysis; no cord felt palpable; epidural block adequate
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Repeat McRoberts hyperflexion and suprapubic pressure for another minute with more forceful application by all available assistants before escalating further
options.rationale: Repeat cycles of the same manoeuvre waste time; the HELPERR pathway moves promptly to internal manoeuvres after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed. Fetal head-to-body delivery interval predicts acidosis and injury. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Deliver the posterior arm by inserting a hand along the fetal back and sweeping it across the chest to bring the posterior arm out first
options.rationale: Delivery of the posterior arm is the RANZCOG next step after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure fails; it converts the bisacromial diameter to the more favourable acromio-axillary and has the highest resolution rate of the internal manoeuvres. Rubin II and Woods screw are alternative internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Apply fundal pressure while continuing suprapubic pressure to overcome the impaction and deliver the anterior shoulder without episiotomy
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury risk. It should never be used. Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) is different. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Perform symphysiotomy under local infiltration to widen the pelvic outlet before attempting further shoulder manoeuvres or Zavanelli manoeuvre
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre in Australian obstetric practice after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; it carries significant maternal morbidity and is not the next step after McRoberts fails. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre replacing the head into the pelvis and proceeding immediately to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; skipping directly to it is inappropriate at this stage where internal manoeuvres have not yet been attempted. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: This is shoulder dystocia. The RANZCOG HELPERR pathway is Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres including Rubin II and Woods), Remove posterior arm, and Roll patient to all-fours. After McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed, delivery of the posterior arm is the next-highest-yielding internal manoeuvre. Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED and Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last resorts after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery fail.
key_points: HELPERR sequence for shoulder dystocia
After McRoberts plus SPP: internal manoeuvres or posterior arm delivery
Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED (worsens impaction, brachial plexus injury)
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last-resort
explanation.pearls: In shoulder dystocia after failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, do NOT repeat the same manoeuvre; move directly to the posterior arm which has the highest resolution rate.

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption vs praevia discrimination and management
stem:
A 31-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 33 plus 2 weeks presents to your regional birth suite with 2 hours of severe constant lower abdominal pain and moderate dark vaginal bleeding. She has had two previous uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her booking anatomy scan at 20 weeks reported a posterior fundal placenta with the lower edge well clear of the internal cervical os. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily and had a fall from a low horse this morning.

On arrival she is anxious with a firm tender uterus that palpates as woody hard on abdominal examination. She is unable to feel fetal movements over the last hour. Speculum examination has been deferred due to the known posterior placental position and abdominal tenderness. IV access has been secured with two large-bore cannulae and full antenatal haemorrhage protocol activated.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C; fetal HR 88 on doptone with prolonged decelerations
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen woody hard tender uterus at 34 cm; scant dark vaginal blood at introitus; no visible source outside vaginal orifice
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (booking 128); INR 1.4 fibrinogen 1.8 g/L; blood group A rhesus negative; Kleihauer-Betke pending; formal ultrasound pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer 250 micrograms of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin, transfuse two units of packed red cells, and admit for close observation with tocolysis
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in placental abruption because it can worsen bleeding and hide clinical deterioration. Anti-D and transfusion should be given but are supportive; the primary need is delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Perform digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before proceeding to expectant management with continuous cardiotocography and 6 hourly review
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination in undiagnosed antepartum haemorrhage before excluding praevia risks catastrophic bleeding; ultrasound must precede a digital exam. Expectant management is inappropriate given fetal compromise and maternal shock. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Give intramuscular corticosteroid for foetal lung maturation and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before category one caesarean section under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean should not be delayed for steroid or magnesium administration when there is severe abruption with fetal compromise; steroids given intraoperatively (which is common practice) do not delay delivery. Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated by the coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Continuous cardiotocography, bolus intravenous crystalloid, activate massive transfusion protocol and proceed to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: This is placental abruption (constant pain, woody uterus, dark blood, maternal shock, coagulopathy) with fetal compromise (fetal HR 88 with prolonged decelerations). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean when there is maternal or fetal compromise from abruption. Resuscitation and MTP activation occur in parallel with theatre transfer. GA is preferred over neuraxial when there is coagulopathy (fibrinogen 1.8, INR 1.4). (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Await emergency transabdominal ultrasound scan to confirm placental location and grade the abruption before making a decision about mode and timing of delivery
options.rationale: Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption (misses up to 50 percent) and is not diagnostic; delaying delivery for imaging in the face of fetal bradycardia and maternal shock costs the baby. Clinical picture of abruption plus fetal compromise mandates immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

explanation.summary: The clinical picture (constant pain, woody uterus, dark bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, fetal bradycardia) is placental abruption with maternal and fetal compromise. RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean in this setting; resuscitation, MTP activation, and theatre transfer occur in parallel. GA is preferred over regional anaesthesia given the coagulopathy. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated before excluding praevia, ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption, and tocolysis is contraindicated.
key_points: Abruption + maternal/fetal compromise = category 1 caesarean
GA preferred if coagulopathy (fibrinogen <2 g/L, INR >1.4)
Ultrasound misses up to 50 percent of abruptions - do not delay for imaging
Tocolysis contraindicated in abruption
explanation.pearls: A woody hard tender uterus with dark PV bleeding and fetal bradycardia is abruption until proved otherwise; go to theatre with MTP activated, do not wait for ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: Second twin delivery with non-cephalic presentation
stem:
A 30-year-old gravida 2 para 1 at 37 plus 4 weeks with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is in your tertiary birth suite. Both twins were cephalic at 36 weeks. Twin one was delivered spontaneously vaginally 8 minutes ago after an uncomplicated first stage of labour, birth weight 2820 g, Apgars 8 and 9. The consultant obstetrician and neonatology team are present.

Ultrasound immediately after twin one delivery shows twin two now in a transverse lie with the back inferior and a longitudinal spine. Cardiotocograph of twin two shows a reassuring reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. The membranes of twin two are intact. She is comfortable with a working epidural and the birthing team has been briefed. Vital signs are within normal limits. The team has been briefed and options for intrapartum management have been thoroughly discussed antenatally.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 88, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air; twin 2 fetal HR 145 reactive with moderate variability
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft with palpable transverse fetal lie of twin 2, back inferior; cervix fully dilated; membranes intact; longitudinal spine confirmed on ultrasound
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound: transverse lie of twin 2 with back inferior; placenta not previa; amniotic fluid adequate; no cord presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mode of delivery for twin two?

options.text: External cephalic version to cephalic under continuous ultrasound guidance followed by amniotomy and spontaneous vaginal delivery of twin 2
options.rationale: External cephalic version of a second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres in this setting and risks umbilical cord accidents from a transverse position with intact membranes. Internal podalic version is the preferred approach in an experienced unit for non-cephalic second twin. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Amniotomy of twin 2 sac now and await spontaneous descent while continuous cardiotocography assesses fetal wellbeing over the next 60 minutes
options.rationale: Amniotomy without version in a transverse lie risks cord prolapse or arm prolapse; the fetus will not descend from a transverse position. Delaying delivery of the second twin beyond about 30 minutes also increases neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Immediate emergency category one caesarean section for twin 2 under regional anaesthesia after early counselling of the mother
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean of the second twin after vaginal delivery of the first carries substantial maternal morbidity (combined vaginal and caesarean recovery); it is reserved for cases where internal manoeuvres are not feasible or fetal compromise supervenes. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Internal podalic version and breech extraction with intact membranes broken as the fetal foot is delivered through the cervix
options.rationale: For a non-cephalic second twin at term in an experienced unit, internal podalic version with breech extraction (grasping a fetal foot and bringing it down before amniotomy) has better outcomes than ECV or immediate caesarean when the CTG is reassuring. This is the RANZCOG-endorsed approach when the accoucheur is experienced. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)
