options.text: Commence oxytocin augmentation to encourage descent of twin 2 with amniotomy at the next contraction under regional block with continuous cardiotocography
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation for a transverse lie is not standard practice and will not correct the presentation. Amniotomy without version risks cord or arm prolapse from the transverse position. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: This is a twin two now in transverse lie after vaginal delivery of a cephalic twin one, with a reassuring CTG and intact membranes in a term dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy. RANZCOG endorses internal podalic version with breech extraction as the optimal approach in an experienced unit: the accoucheur grasps a fetal foot, brings it down, and performs breech extraction only breaking membranes at the last moment. This avoids the maternal morbidity of caesarean after vaginal delivery and has better outcomes than ECV, amniotomy without version, or awaiting spontaneous descent.
key_points: Internal podalic version + breech extraction is preferred for non-cephalic second twin
Break membranes as the foot is brought through, not before, to avoid cord prolapse
ECV of second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres
Delivery of twin 2 within 30 minutes of twin 1 minimises neonatal morbidity
explanation.pearls: For a transverse second twin with reassuring CTG at term, internal podalic version by an experienced accoucheur beats caesarean; keep the membranes intact until you have a foot through the cervix.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition and resuscitation
stem:
A 34-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 39 plus 2 weeks is having oxytocin augmentation for prolonged second stage. Ten minutes after artificial rupture of membranes she becomes acutely short of breath, agitated, and cyanotic. She then loses consciousness and becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse. The rhythm on the monitor is a narrow-complex PEA. She has no known medical or obstetric history. The baby's head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated.

The arrest team is called and CPR is commenced. The consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist, neonatology team, and haematology are on their way. There is early bright red PV bleeding estimated at 300 mL and increasing. Bedside coagulation testing reveals INR 3.2 and fibrinogen 0.6 g/L. Left lateral tilt has been applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal cardiac arrest, PEA on monitor, no palpable pulse; fetal HR 60 on doppler decreasing
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive; CPR in progress; cyanotic; fresh bright red PV bleed 300 mL and increasing; uterus soft; head at station +2 with cervix fully dilated
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care coags INR 3.2 fibrinogen 0.6 g/L; venous gas pH 7.10 lactate 8 mmol/L; haemoglobin 78 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Continue CPR and administer intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram then deliver the baby by perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes of arrest
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes is standard for maternal arrest at more than 20 weeks WHEN vaginal delivery is not imminent. Here the head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated; a category 1 assisted vaginal delivery (rotational forceps or ventouse) achieves delivery faster than caesarean and improves both maternal and fetal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG maternal collapse statement)

options.text: Continue CPR and administer intravenous fibrinogen concentrate 4 grams and cryoprecipitate as the primary resuscitation without delivering the baby immediately
options.rationale: Blood products are essential and should be given but delaying delivery is worse; delivery relieves aortocaval compression and dramatically improves resuscitation chances. Blood products and delivery happen together, not sequentially. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give a 30 millilitre per kilogram bolus of Hartmann's solution, and administer intravenous salbutamol 250 micrograms bolus to reverse bronchospasm
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not part of the AFE resuscitation algorithm; the mechanism is not primarily bronchospasm but multiorgan haemodynamic collapse and DIC. Fluid without blood products in massive haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give thrombolysis with alteplase 100 milligrams intravenously over 2 hours for presumed pulmonary embolism during pregnancy
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in a peripartum patient with already severe coagulopathy and active haemorrhage is catastrophic. The clinical picture is AFE (sudden collapse with DIC) not PE (which usually presents with unilateral leg findings, pleuritic pain, and different haemodynamics). (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram, activate massive transfusion, and perform immediate assisted vaginal delivery by ventouse or forceps
options.rationale: This is amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac arrest AND imminent vaginal delivery (station +2, fully dilated). ANZCOR maternal cardiac arrest algorithm calls for delivery within 4-5 minutes to improve maternal circulation; when vaginal delivery is imminent, assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. MTP activation and standard ALS with adrenaline continue in parallel. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

explanation.summary: This is amniotic fluid embolism (sudden peripartum collapse with cardiac arrest and DIC after ARM). The ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest algorithm mandates delivery within 4-5 minutes to relieve aortocaval compression and improve circulation. When vaginal delivery is imminent (fully dilated, head at station +2), assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. Standard ALS (chest compressions, adrenaline 1 mg, defibrillation for shockable rhythms) and MTP activation with balanced blood products for DIC occur in parallel. Fluid alone worsens coagulopathy; thrombolysis is contraindicated with active haemorrhage.
key_points: AFE presents with sudden collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC
Delivery within 4-5 minutes of arrest improves resuscitation
Assisted vaginal delivery preferred if fully dilated and station +2 or lower
MTP with balanced blood products for the DIC; avoid crystalloid-only resuscitation
explanation.pearls: In maternal cardiac arrest with cervix fully dilated and head at station +2, an emergency ventouse or forceps beats perimortem caesarean because it delivers faster with less blood loss.

stem:
A 72-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VA of 4 presents to your regional emergency department with 2 hours of a sudden severe headache with vomiting and left sided weakness. He last took his warfarin 12 hours ago. He has no history of hepatic impairment. He usually runs an INR between 2.0 and 3.0.

On arrival he is GCS 12 with dysarthria, a left facial droop, and left arm 3/5 power. A non-contrast CT head confirms a 5 cm right basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage with 4 mm of midline shift. Blood pressure is 178/104 and haemodynamics are otherwise stable. IV access has been secured. He is nil by mouth pending neurosurgery review.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 irregular, BP 178/104, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Alert to voice; dysarthria; left facial droop; left arm 3/5 power; leg 4/5; no meningism; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.2; APTT 42 seconds; haemoglobin 132 g/L; platelets 220 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 3.4 g/L; sodium 140 potassium 4.2 creatinine 96; CT head as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal regimen?

options.text: Vitamin K 10 milligrams intravenously alone with hourly INR monitoring for the next 4 hours before considering further reversal treatment
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6-12 hours to lower INR meaningfully and does not immediately restore clotting factors; in life-threatening bleeding, prothrombinex is needed to achieve factor replacement within minutes. Vitamin K must still be given but as an adjunct, not sole therapy. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Prothrombinex-VF 50 international units per kilogram intravenously plus vitamin K 5 to 10 milligrams intravenously with repeat INR at 30 minutes
options.rationale: NBA Australian warfarin reversal for life-threatening bleeding (including intracerebral haemorrhage) is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV (weight-banded in some protocols) plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; add fresh frozen plasma 150-300 mL if prothrombinex is unavailable or if the INR remains elevated. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 millilitres per kilogram alone without prothrombinex and vitamin K 1 milligram orally with repeat INR at 6 hours
options.rationale: FFP alone requires 4-6 units for adequate factor replacement, has slower onset than prothrombinex, and carries greater volume load; prothrombinex is preferred first-line in AU practice. Oral vitamin K is not appropriate in life-threatening bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms per kilogram intravenously as the primary reversal agent given the intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not in the NBA warfarin reversal pathway; it carries substantial thrombotic risk and is not indicated for warfarin reversal. Prothrombinex plus vitamin K is the AU first-line for life-threatening warfarin-related bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 grams intravenously in two 2.5 gram doses as immediate specific reversal agent for the anticoagulant effect
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a specific dabigatran reversal agent, not warfarin. Using it for warfarin gives no reversal effect and delays appropriate prothrombinex plus vitamin K administration. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

explanation.summary: This is warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage requiring immediate reversal. The NBA Australian pathway for life-threatening bleeding on warfarin is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; FFP is added if prothrombinex is unavailable or if INR remains elevated. Vitamin K alone is too slow, FFP alone has slower onset and volume risk, recombinant factor VIIa is not indicated for warfarin, and idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
key_points: NBA warfarin reversal (life-threatening bleed): prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV
Repeat INR at 30 minutes and re-dose if needed
FFP is second-line or add-on, not first-line in Australia
Idarucizumab is dabigatran reversal, not warfarin
explanation.pearls: For any warfarin-related intracranial haemorrhage, prothrombinex 50 IU/kg plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV within 30 minutes is your target; do not spend the first hour on FFP alone.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3 presents to your district hospital emergency department with 2 days of increasing dysuria, frank haematuria, and 6 hours of rigors. She had a right ureteric stent placed 3 weeks ago for an obstructing stone. She has been drinking 3 litres of water daily.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and haemodynamically compromised. Her right renal angle is tender. There is no rash. IV access has been secured with an 18 gauge cannula. The nurse has just returned from taking blood cultures and a serum lactate. Vital signs and gas results have just come back.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; mottled peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds; right renal angle tender; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.6 mmol/L base excess -8; white cell count 21 x10^9/L neutrophils 18; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 130); urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive; bedside urine microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes and commence peripheral noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute immediately before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Vasopressors are added when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate fluid resuscitation, not started before antibiotics. Antibiotic priority in the first hour is paramount for shock outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours first then administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams once the bolus is completed
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics for 3 hours is inconsistent with the hour-1 bundle, which mandates antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition. Fluid and antibiotics run in parallel, not sequentially. Ceftriaxone monotherapy also under-covers resistant post-stent flora. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 grams plus gentamicin 5 milligrams per kilogram now followed by a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle: give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition, and start a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate above 4. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers Gram-negative and Gram-positive urosepsis and the resistant flora often present after a recent stent. Vasopressors are added if MAP under 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT KUB and defer antibiotic administration until obstruction is confirmed and urology has assessed for immediate stent revision
options.rationale: Imaging is important to identify source control needs but must not delay antibiotics or resuscitation in septic shock; antibiotics and fluids run first, imaging follows. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous meropenem 1 gram as monotherapy and 500 millilitres of Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes before repeat vital signs assessment at 1 hour
options.rationale: 500 mL bolus is well under the 30 mL/kg recommended for septic shock; underfluid resuscitation prolongs shock. Meropenem monotherapy is broader than typically needed for urosepsis in Australia (eTG piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin is the standard). (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This is septic shock from urosepsis in a patient with a recent ureteric stent, complicated by acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis. The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition, blood cultures before antibiotics (already taken), lactate measurement, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4. Vasopressors are added when MAP stays under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers resistant post-stent urosepsis flora. Imaging and source control follow antibiotics and resuscitation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >4 mmol/L
Vasopressors added when MAP <65 after fluid resuscitation
Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for post-stent urosepsis (eTG)
explanation.pearls: In septic shock, antibiotics and fluids run in parallel within the first hour; save vasopressors for after fluid, and never delay antibiotics for imaging or source control planning.

stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to your general medicine outpatient clinic for review after a low-trauma right distal radius fracture 6 weeks ago after tripping on a garden hose. She takes ramipril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no other medical history. She has no history of oesophageal disease and swallows tablets easily.

Her dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan (DXA) at the femoral neck shows a T score of -2.9 and at lumbar spine -2.6. Her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 62 nmol/L and corrected calcium is 2.32 mmol/L. Renal function is normal with an eGFR of 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. She is willing to accept an oral therapy and lives with her husband who can help her with dosing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; well healed distal radius fracture with plaster removed 2 weeks ago; no proximal myopathy or bone tenderness elsewhere; no dental disease
data_table.Investigations: DXA femoral neck T -2.9 lumbar spine T -2.6; 25-OH-vitamin D 62 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L; creatinine 68 eGFR 78; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral strontium ranelate 2 grams daily dissolved in water at bedtime with attention to cardiovascular risk factors and periodic cardiovascular review
options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn or restricted in many jurisdictions because of cardiovascular risk and has fallen out of first-line use. It is not the AU first-line for osteoporosis. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 milligrams every 6 months as first-line with strict adherence to schedule to avoid rebound bone loss on discontinuation
options.rationale: Denosumab is very effective but is not routine first-line in Australia because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; PBS restriction is for patients who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to oral bisphosphonates. It is preferred second-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms daily for up to 24 months as anabolic therapy given the low T score at both femoral neck and lumbar spine
options.rationale: Teriparatide is a PBS-restricted anabolic reserved for very high fracture risk (T score under -3.0 with 2 or more fractures on bisphosphonate) or for severe glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; first-line therapy is oral alendronate for this patient. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 milligrams weekly with instructions to remain upright for 30 minutes after each dose and take vitamin D 1000 international units daily
options.rationale: For postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma fracture and T score under -2.5, alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line per Australian osteoporosis guidance because it is inexpensive, PBS-listed, and has robust anti-fracture data. Take upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium sufficient at baseline. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 milligrams daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with attention to hot flushes and venous thromboembolism risk
options.rationale: Raloxifene is a second or third-line option and increases venous thromboembolism risk; it is not first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture. Bisphosphonate is preferred first-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma distal radius fracture and T scores under -2.5 at the femoral neck and lumbar spine. Australian first-line pharmacotherapy is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly), taken upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium are adequate at baseline. Denosumab is second-line due to rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; teriparatide is reserved for very high risk patients; strontium ranelate has been restricted for cardiovascular reasons; and raloxifene is a later-line SERM.
key_points: First-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal-trauma fracture: oral bisphosphonate
Take alendronate 70 mg weekly upright 30 min before food with water
Denosumab has rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation
Teriparatide reserved for very high risk (T -3.0 with 2+ fractures on bisphosphonate)
explanation.pearls: For a first fragility fracture with a T score of -2.5 or worse, oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is the AU default; save denosumab for oral intolerance or contraindication.

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection type discrimination and initial management
stem:
A 58-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your metropolitan emergency department with sudden onset of tearing interscapular chest pain radiating to his back 60 minutes ago. He is a current smoker and has a strong family history of aortic aneurysm. He denies syncope. His pulses are palpable in both radial arteries with a difference in blood pressure of 24 mmHg between arms.

On arrival he is diaphoretic and anxious. Cardiovascular examination reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and equal bilateral chest expansion with air entry. There is no focal neurology or abdominal pain. IV access has been secured. A CT angiogram of the aorta has just returned and shows an intimal flap starting at the ascending aorta and extending distally past the arch into the descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta beyond the coeliac axis, without extension into the coronary ostia or a pericardial effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 176/98 right arm and 152/86 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; anxious; early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; equal bilateral chest expansion; abdomen soft; distal pulses palpable and equal
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ischaemic change; troponin negative; chest X-ray widened mediastinum; CT aortogram as described in stem

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate under 60 followed by intravenous sodium nitroprusside to systolic under 120 mmHg with cardiothoracic referral
options.rationale: This is a Stanford type A dissection (starts in ascending aorta) and is a surgical emergency; medical management aims to reduce shear stress with beta-blockade FIRST to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator to bring systolic BP to about 100-120 mmHg while awaiting operative repair. Nitroprusside without prior beta-blockade risks reflex tachycardia worsening shear stress. Aortic root repair is definitive. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 milligrams bolus and admit under vascular for medical management alone as this is a Stanford type B dissection amenable to conservative therapy
options.rationale: The flap starts in the ascending aorta making this Stanford type A, not type B. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency (30 percent mortality per day untreated) not amenable to medical management alone. Labetalol is appropriate but the disposition is theatre, not conservative admission. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight-based dosing intravenously for presumed anterior STEMI with new murmur suggestive of papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in aortic dissection is catastrophic (accelerates the dissection and causes tamponade or exsanguination). The tearing pain radiating to the back plus widened mediastinum plus BP asymmetry point to dissection not STEMI, and the ECG is not diagnostic of STEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous morphine and oral aspirin 300 milligrams then clopidogrel 300 milligrams with admission to coronary care unit for further workup and troponin trending
options.rationale: Aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy in aortic dissection worsens haemorrhage and delays operative repair. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet loading are contraindicated. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure under 140 with intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams for the diastolic murmur suggestive of acute aortic regurgitation
options.rationale: Nitrate without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and worsens dissection propagation; the priority is beta-blockade first (esmolol or labetalol) then a vasodilator. Furosemide is not indicated in dissection unless overt pulmonary oedema is present. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: This is Stanford type A aortic dissection (flap starts in the ascending aorta) with aortic regurgitation and BP asymmetry. Type A is a surgical emergency with mortality of 1 percent per hour untreated. Medical bridging aims to reduce shear stress: beta-blocker FIRST (esmolol infusion to HR under 60) to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) to bring systolic BP to 100-120 mmHg while cardiothoracic surgery is arranged. Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens propagation. Antiplatelet loading, thrombolysis, and diuretic-first strategies are all incorrect and harmful.
key_points: Type A dissection = surgical emergency; type B usually medical
Medical bridging: beta-blocker first (HR <60), then vasodilator (SBP 100-120)
Antiplatelet loading and thrombolysis are contraindicated
Vasodilator without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and propagation
explanation.pearls: In aortic dissection, always beta-block BEFORE giving nitroprusside; giving nitroprusside first causes reflex tachycardia that extends the flap.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity presents to your regional emergency department with 24 hours of increasing right calf pain that has become disproportionate to the clinical findings. He recalled scratching his leg on garden wire 4 days ago. His pain has escalated despite oral paracetamol and now feels excruciating on light touch.

On examination there is a small area of erythema on the anterior right calf with hazy dusky discoloration extending beyond the erythematous border and a single haemorrhagic bulla. Sensation over the affected area is reduced. He has palpable pedal pulses and no obvious crepitus. He is drowsy and diaphoretic with cool peripheries. IV access has been secured and initial resuscitation has commenced with fluids and cultures drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/58 (MAP 71), RR 26, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; right calf with area of erythema, dusky discoloration beyond the erythematous border, one haemorrhagic bulla, reduced sensation, no crepitus; palpable pedal pulses; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22 x10^9/L; sodium 132 potassium 4.4 creatinine 148 (baseline 90) urea 12; glucose 18.2 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.4; CRP 380 mg/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the lower limb to confirm gas in the tissue planes before any surgical review is arranged
options.rationale: Imaging is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain but should NEVER delay surgical review or theatre when clinical features and LRINEC are strongly suggestive; absence of gas on imaging does NOT exclude nec fasc. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 grams 6 hourly and mark the erythema border with observation for 4 hours before deciding on surgical review or escalation
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis and does not suppress streptococcal toxin production. Watching and waiting is fatal in nec fasc; the LRINEC of 8 and clinical picture mandate immediate surgery. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams and elevate the limb with strict bed rest for cellulitis treatment while awaiting orthopaedic surgical review the next morning
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is insufficient for nec fasc and treating this as cellulitis with elective review delays theatre. Overnight delay in a septic nec fasc patient is fatal. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Immediate surgical review with plan for urgent theatre debridement plus intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin as empirical antibiotic cover
options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, hazy dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8) with sepsis. Definitive management is EARLY surgical debridement in theatre alongside broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin is the standard eTG Australian empirical regimen. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy with 100 percent oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres for 90 minutes as adjunctive treatment before the first surgical debridement is performed
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may be an adjunct AFTER surgical debridement and antibiotics; it does NOT replace or precede surgery. Delaying debridement to arrange HBO is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: This is necrotising fasciitis with sepsis (pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8). Management is IMMEDIATE surgical debridement plus broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for streptococcal toxin suppression. The eTG empirical regimen is piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin (for MRSA) plus clindamycin. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality; imaging should not delay theatre when clinical features are strong. HBO is an adjunct at best, not a substitute for surgery.
key_points: Nec fasc clinical clues: pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, bullae, sensory loss
LRINEC score >=8 is high probability
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Immediate surgical debridement is the cornerstone; imaging must not delay theatre
explanation.pearls: In suspected nec fasc, activate theatre before finalising imaging; the LRINEC and clinical picture are enough, and every hour of delay adds mortality.

sources.label: ANZAS surgical guidelines: Necrotising soft tissue infection

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis refractory to first-line adrenaline
stem:
A 62-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis attends an infusion suite for her scheduled infliximab infusion. She takes metoprolol 100 mg twice daily for chronic atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate. Within 10 minutes of starting the infusion she develops generalised urticaria, wheeze, and hypotension.

The infusion has been stopped, she has been laid flat, and she has received one dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh. Five minutes later she remains hypotensive with persistent wheeze and hoarse voice. She has just received a second dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms. She has IV access with two large-bore cannulae. She has been given 1 litre of Hartmann's solution over the last 5 minutes and is on 6 L/min via Hudson mask.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 82/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; audible wheeze; hoarse voice; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.30 lactate 3.4 mmol/L; ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response at 82

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Third intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms and continue 500 millilitre crystalloid boluses to a maximum of 4 litres before considering additional agents
options.rationale: After two IM doses without response, ASCIA advises escalating to IV adrenaline infusion rather than a third IM. Continuing crystalloid without escalation of adrenaline delays effective treatment. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to blood pressure and heart rate, and give intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 milligrams for beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance
options.rationale: After two IM adrenaline doses without adequate response, ASCIA recommends IV adrenaline infusion. In a patient on beta-blockers who is failing to respond, IV glucagon 1-2 mg (which acts on cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors) is the standard adjunct to overcome beta-blocker resistance. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 milligrams and intravenous chlorpheniramine 10 milligrams as the primary treatment while the current adrenaline effect is assessed
options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and do not treat the acute cardiovascular collapse; they should not delay escalation to IV adrenaline in refractory anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute infusion as first-line vasopressor for refractory anaphylaxis with continued crystalloid at 250 millilitres per hour
options.rationale: Noradrenaline can be used as adjunct for refractory anaphylactic shock unresponsive to adrenaline, but IV adrenaline infusion is the first escalation after IM failure. Skipping adrenaline for noradrenaline is not standard. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 with hydrocortisone 200 milligrams IV and salbutamol 5 milligrams nebuliser as combined therapy for airway symptoms
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but does not treat systemic anaphylactic shock; salbutamol and hydrocortisone are adjuncts. None of these address the beta-blocker-mediated adrenaline resistance that is the barrier here. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is anaphylaxis refractory to two IM adrenaline doses in a patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy. ASCIA escalates to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response after two IM doses fail. When beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance is suspected, IV glucagon 1-2 mg is the standard adjunct because it increases cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors. Steroids, antihistamines, nebulised adrenaline, and noradrenaline all have supporting or adjunct roles but do not replace escalation of adrenaline and glucagon in this scenario.
key_points: After 2 IM adrenaline doses without response: IV adrenaline infusion
Beta-blocker on board: give IV glucagon 1-2 mg for adrenaline resistance
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not primary treatment
Noradrenaline is a later add-on for refractory shock unresponsive to adrenaline
explanation.pearls: In an anaphylactic patient on beta-blockers not responding to IM adrenaline, IV glucagon 1-2 mg alongside IV adrenaline infusion is the way to unlock the beta-adrenergic blockade.

stem:
A 42-year-old man newly diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma is admitted to your haematology ward for CODOX-M induction chemotherapy. He has bulky abdominal disease, a serum lactate dehydrogenase over four times the upper limit of normal, and a white cell count of 68 x10^9/L. He is of African heritage and has no known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; his G6PD screen has just returned as normal.

His serum uric acid is 0.55 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, and creatinine 108 micromol/L. He has received 3 litres of intravenous Hartmann's solution over the last 12 hours and his urine output has been 100 mL per hour. Chemotherapy is planned to start within the next 12 hours. He weighs 72 kilograms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; palpable bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly with liver 6 cm below costal margin; no rash; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Uric acid 0.55 mmol/L; corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; phosphate 1.6 mmol/L; potassium 4.8 mmol/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L; LDH 1620 U/L; white cell count 68 x10^9/L; G6PD screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis?

options.text: Oral allopurinol 300 milligrams daily and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Allopurinol prevents new uric acid formation but does NOT treat the existing high uric acid; it takes 48-72 hours to lower urate meaningfully. For high-risk TLS (Burkitt with bulky disease, LDH >4 times upper limit, and baseline urate above upper limit) rasburicase is preferred as it degrades existing uric acid within hours. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Prophylactic haemodialysis prior to induction chemotherapy with a target urea reduction ratio of 65 percent before the first dose of chemotherapy
options.rationale: Prophylactic dialysis is only indicated when established renal failure or refractory hyperkalaemia or hyperphosphataemia occurs during TLS; it is not routine prophylaxis. Rasburicase plus aggressive hydration prevents most cases from progressing to dialysis. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Oral febuxostat 80 milligrams daily and sodium bicarbonate infusion to urinary pH above 7.5 with intravenous crystalloid at 4 litres per square metre daily
options.rationale: Febuxostat is an alternative to allopurinol but is not preferred over rasburicase for high-risk TLS. Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NO LONGER recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation and increases xanthine crystallisation. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Intravenous rasburicase 0.2 milligrams per kilogram single dose and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring
options.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and elevated baseline uric acid places this patient in the high-risk TLS category. eviQ and HSANZ pathways recommend rasburicase as first-line uric acid lowering because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation. G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk) has been excluded. Hyperhydration with balanced crystalloid continues. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Delay induction chemotherapy for 48 hours and commence oral allopurinol 300 milligrams three times daily with sodium bicarbonate infusion for urinary alkalinisation
options.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma has extremely rapid doubling time; delaying chemotherapy for prophylaxis without addressing the immediate uric acid risk is dangerous. Rasburicase allows chemotherapy to start on schedule while managing hyperuricaemia. Alkalinisation is not recommended. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

explanation.summary: This patient is high-risk for TLS (Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and baseline uric acid above upper limit). eviQ and HSANZ recommend rasburicase (0.2 mg/kg IV as a single dose or a fixed-dose regimen) for high-risk TLS because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation and takes 48-72 hours. G6PD deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase due to haemolysis risk; screening was normal here. Hyperhydration continues but urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is no longer recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation. Prophylactic dialysis is not routine.
key_points: High-risk TLS (Burkitt, bulky disease, LDH >4x ULN, high urate): rasburicase
Screen G6PD before rasburicase (contraindicated in deficiency)
Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NOT recommended
Allopurinol only blocks new urate formation; slow onset (48-72 hours)
explanation.pearls: For high-risk TLS in Burkitt lymphoma with a G6PD-normal patient, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV drops existing urate within hours; do not waste time on allopurinol prophylaxis alone.

stem:
A 26-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 18 days, titrated up to a current dose of 300 mg daily. He presents to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service with 2 days of fever, tachycardia, and generalised fatigue. He denies chest pain but reports mild shortness of breath on climbing stairs, which is new. There is no cough or productive sputum.

On examination he looks systemically unwell. There is a soft third heart sound on auscultation with no murmur, no peripheral oedema, and mild bibasal crackles. Chest is otherwise clear. Neutrophil count is within normal limits. His clozapine level is 400 micrograms per litre.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/68, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; fatigued; soft third heart sound; no murmur; no peripheral oedema; mild bibasal crackles; chest otherwise clear; no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L neutrophils 5.6; CRP 82 mg/L; troponin I 480 ng/L (upper limit 26); NT-pro-BNP 3400 pg/mL; ECG shows sinus tachycardia with widespread T wave inversion; chest X-ray shows mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette without pulmonary oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram plus cardiology review with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging if echocardiogram is abnormal
options.rationale: The clinical picture (initiation window at 2-4 weeks, fever, tachycardia, raised troponin and BNP, ECG changes) is clozapine-induced myocarditis. Australian clozapine protocols mandate immediate cessation, cardiology review, echocardiogram, and cardiac MRI. Rechallenge is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose and start empirical intravenous ceftriaxone plus vancomycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia or infective endocarditis
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics without evidence of infection miss the diagnosis of myocarditis and expose the patient to unnecessary antibiotics; continuing clozapine in confirmed or suspected myocarditis worsens outcomes. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose to 150 milligrams and repeat troponin and echocardiogram in 72 hours before deciding on definitive cessation of therapy
options.rationale: Dose reduction is not adequate management of clozapine myocarditis; immediate cessation is required. Continuing at any dose risks progression to cardiogenic shock or death. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

options.text: Continue clozapine and add oral aspirin 100 milligrams and oral atorvastatin 40 milligrams for presumed acute coronary syndrome in a young smoker
options.rationale: This is not acute coronary syndrome (young, no chest pain, widespread T-wave changes and initiation timing point to myocarditis). ACS pathway does not address clozapine cessation which is the priority. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

options.text: Withhold clozapine for 48 hours and restart at the same dose if the patient defervesces and the troponin trends downward on repeat testing
options.rationale: Even brief re-exposure risks recurrence; the rule after suspected clozapine myocarditis is permanent cessation and formal cardiology assessment, not empirical rechallenge. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

explanation.summary: Clozapine myocarditis characteristically occurs in the first 4-6 weeks of initiation with fever, tachycardia, raised troponin, raised BNP, ECG changes, and reduced left ventricular function on echocardiogram. Australian protocols mandate baseline and weekly troponin, BNP, and CRP for the first 4 weeks. Suspected myocarditis requires immediate clozapine cessation, cardiology review, echocardiogram, and cardiac MRI. Rechallenge is contraindicated in confirmed myocarditis. Dose reduction, continuing therapy, or empirical antibiotics all miss the diagnosis and delay definitive management.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis window: first 4-6 weeks of initiation
Screen with troponin, BNP, CRP weekly for first 4 weeks in AU protocols
Confirmed or suspected myocarditis: immediate cessation, cardiology review
Rechallenge is contraindicated after myocarditis
explanation.pearls: Fever plus tachycardia plus raised troponin in weeks 2-4 of clozapine is myocarditis until proved otherwise; stop it immediately and never rechallenge.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 900 mg daily for 15 years presents to your emergency department with 4 days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and confusion after a gastroenteritis illness. Her partner reports she has been more unsteady on her feet over the last 48 hours. She recently started perindopril 4 mg daily for hypertension.

On examination she is confused with coarse tremor, fasciculations at the shoulders and thighs, and marked ataxia. Reflexes are hyperactive with sustained clonus at the ankles bilaterally. There is no focal neurology and pupils are equal. Serum lithium level, taken 8 hours after her last dose, is 3.6 mmol/L. Creatinine is 180 micromol/L (baseline 82). She has been catheterised with urine output of 20 mL over 2 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 108/68, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Confused (GCS 14); coarse tremor with fasciculations; marked ataxia; hyperreflexia with sustained clonus; pupils equal and reactive; no focal weakness; skin turgor reduced
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 3.6 mmol/L (target 0.4-1.0 mmol/L); sodium 148 potassium 4.2 urea 14 creatinine 180 (baseline 82); venous gas pH 7.42 lactate 2.1 mmol/L; TSH 5.2 mIU/L; ECG sinus rhythm with prolonged QT 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lithium, commence intravenous normal saline at 200 millilitres per hour, and admit for observation without initiating haemodialysis at this stage
options.rationale: Lithium 3.6 mmol/L with acute-on-chronic toxicity, severe neurological symptoms, and acute kidney injury meets Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning workgroup (EXTRIP) criteria for haemodialysis. Fluid alone is insufficient with reduced clearance and continuing neurotoxicity. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

options.text: Cease lithium, cease perindopril, commence intravenous normal saline resuscitation, arrange urgent intermittent haemodialysis, and consult toxicology and renal
options.rationale: EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis in lithium toxicity: level above 4 mmol/L OR level 2.5-4 mmol/L with severe symptoms (impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia) OR acute kidney injury reducing lithium clearance. This patient meets all three qualifying features. Cease all nephrotoxins including ACE inhibitor. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

options.text: Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 450 milligrams daily, give intravenous 5 percent dextrose 2 litres over 12 hours, and repeat lithium level in 24 hours
options.rationale: Continuing lithium at any dose in the setting of acute toxicity with neurotoxicity and AKI is inappropriate. Dextrose is not the appropriate fluid and delaying dialysis in the face of neurological symptoms and reduced clearance risks preventable disability. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 grams orally and observe with fluid resuscitation and antiemetics before deciding on further management at 6 hours
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity; using it delays definitive treatment. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 grams and rectal enema 60 grams to enhance lithium elimination via the gastrointestinal tract
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has been trialled as gut binding but is inferior to dialysis in severe toxicity and carries GI necrosis risk. It is not standard first-line management. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

explanation.summary: This is acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by gastroenteritis, ACE inhibitor introduction, and resulting acute kidney injury. EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis: lithium above 4 mmol/L OR 2.5-4 mmol/L with severe neurological symptoms (impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia) OR acute kidney injury reducing clearance. This patient meets multiple criteria. Cease lithium and all nephrotoxins (including ACE inhibitor), commence isotonic fluid resuscitation, and arrange urgent haemodialysis with toxicology and renal input.
key_points: EXTRIP HD in lithium tox: level >4 OR 2.5-4 with severe symptoms OR AKI
Cease all nephrotoxins including ACE inhibitors and diuretics
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium
Chronic on acute toxicity has higher risk than pure acute at same level
explanation.pearls: Any lithium level above 2.5 mmol/L with AKI and neurotoxicity is a dialysis case; do not chase levels with fluid alone.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is admitted overnight to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service. She has depression on venlafaxine 225 mg daily and has recently been started on tramadol 100 mg four times daily by her general practitioner for lower back pain 3 days ago. Over 6 hours she has become confused, agitated, diaphoretic, and febrile.

On examination she is agitated and restless with dilated pupils. There is marked lower limb hyperreflexia with 5 beats of clonus at the ankles bilaterally. Muscle tone is greater in the lower than upper limbs. She has not received any antipsychotics or antiemetics. There is no rash. She is on IV crystalloid at 125 mL/hr and has had one dose of oral diazepam 10 mg 30 minutes ago without effect.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/104, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and restless; dilated pupils; diaphoretic; lower limb tone increased; hyperreflexia with 5 beats of clonus at ankles bilaterally; upper limbs less affected; no cog-wheel rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L; sodium 138 potassium 4.4 creatinine 92; venous gas pH 7.36 lactate 2.4 mmol/L; TSH 2.1 mIU/L; ECG sinus tachycardia; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current medications and give intravenous paracetamol 1 gram plus rapid external cooling with iced peritoneal lavage for immediate temperature control
options.rationale: Paracetamol does not treat serotonin syndrome or NMS; the temperature is centrally driven. Continuing serotonergic drugs is dangerous. Cooling is a supportive adjunct but must be paired with drug withdrawal and pharmacological treatment. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous bromocriptine 2.5 milligrams four times daily and intravenous dantrolene 2 milligrams per kilogram every 6 hours for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are the NMS treatment. This patient has no antipsychotic exposure, has clonus and hyperreflexia (typical of serotonin syndrome), and lacks the lead-pipe rigidity and marked CK elevation typical of NMS. The clinical picture is serotonin syndrome, not NMS. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Cease venlafaxine and tramadol, give intravenous benzodiazepines titrated to sedation, and give oral cyproheptadine 12 milligrams then 2 milligrams hourly up to 32 milligrams daily
options.rationale: This is serotonin syndrome (Sternbach and Hunter criteria: recent addition of a second serotonergic agent, hyperreflexia with clonus greater in lower limbs, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, dilated pupils). Management is withdrawal of serotonergic agents, aggressive benzodiazepine sedation, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours as an antihistamine and 5-HT2A antagonist. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous haloperidol 5 milligrams for the agitation and add intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams plus vancomycin for presumed sepsis with meningitis
options.rationale: Haloperidol can precipitate NMS in someone already unstable, worsening the picture, and blocks dopamine which is unhelpful here. There is no clinical evidence of sepsis; the picture is serotonergic toxidrome. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous naloxone 0.4 milligrams and IV physostigmine 0.5 milligrams for presumed opioid toxidrome with anticholinergic delirium from the tramadol
options.rationale: Naloxone treats opioid toxicity (miosis and respiratory depression); this picture is mydriatic, hyperreflexic and hyperadrenergic. Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxidrome (dry, warm, red) not this presentation. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: This is serotonin syndrome (SNRI plus tramadol, hyperreflexia with clonus greater in lower limbs, dilated pupils, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, tremor within days of adding the second serotonergic agent). NMS is distinguished by dopamine antagonist exposure, lead-pipe rigidity, marked CK rise, and pupil size usually normal. Management of serotonin syndrome is withdrawal of serotonergic agents, aggressive benzodiazepine sedation, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours. Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS not serotonin syndrome. Haloperidol can precipitate NMS.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus greater in lower limbs, dilated pupils, agitation, within days of new serotonergic drug
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, marked CK rise, dopamine antagonist exposure, over days-weeks
Serotonin syndrome treatment: benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine
NMS treatment: bromocriptine and dantrolene
explanation.pearls: Clonus that is greater in the lower limbs than upper limbs, plus dilated pupils, plus a recent serotonergic drug, is serotonin syndrome; give benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine, not bromocriptine.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy with cardiac history
stem:
A 38-year-old man is referred to your general adult psychiatry outpatient clinic for management of newly diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (combined presentation). He has trialled cognitive behavioural strategies and workplace accommodations over 6 months without adequate response. He now requests pharmacotherapy to help with worsening occupational functioning as a lawyer.

His medical history includes an unprovoked pulmonary embolism 3 years ago (currently off anticoagulation) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosed after a syncopal episode 5 years ago with a septal thickness of 22 mm. He has an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and is under regular cardiology follow-up. Baseline resting blood pressure is 138/86 and heart rate 82.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 138/86, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no dysmorphism; ICD scar in place; JVP not raised; no ankle oedema; apex beat displaced with a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG shows LV hypertrophy and left axis deviation; recent echocardiogram septal thickness 22 mm and preserved LVEF at 60 percent; TSH 1.8 mIU/L; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate release starting at 5 milligrams twice daily titrating to 20 milligrams three times daily with 4 weekly ECG and blood pressure review
options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate and dexamfetamine) are relatively contraindicated in structural heart disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to arrhythmia and outflow tract obstruction risks. Even ECG monitoring does not mitigate the underlying risk in a patient with an ICD. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

options.text: Dexamfetamine 5 milligrams twice daily titrating to 15 milligrams three times daily with weekly cardiology liaison and 4 weekly ECG monitoring throughout titration
options.rationale: Dexamfetamine carries the same stimulant-mediated cardiovascular risks as methylphenidate and is relatively contraindicated in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Cardiology liaison does not overcome the structural risk. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

options.text: Atomoxetine starting at 40 milligrams daily and titrating to 80 milligrams daily after 7 days with 4 weekly review of blood pressure, heart rate, and mood
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and is preferred first-line for adult ADHD when stimulants are contraindicated (structural heart disease, substance-use risk, tics). It still requires BP and HR monitoring but has a favourable risk profile in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared with stimulants. RANZCP guidance endorses atomoxetine in this scenario. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

options.text: Bupropion 150 milligrams sustained release daily titrating to 300 milligrams as first-line non-stimulant with cardiology and neurologist input on seizure and cardiac risk
options.rationale: Bupropion has weak evidence for adult ADHD, lowers seizure threshold, and is not first-line non-stimulant in Australia. Atomoxetine is the preferred non-stimulant when stimulants are contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

options.text: Modafinil 100 milligrams daily titrating to 200 milligrams daily as off-label first-line non-stimulant with regular blood pressure monitoring and cardiology input
options.rationale: Modafinil is used for narcolepsy in Australia; it is off-label for ADHD and has arrhythmogenic risks that make it unsuitable in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Atomoxetine is the RANZCP-preferred non-stimulant. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

explanation.summary: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are relatively contraindicated in structural heart disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to risk of arrhythmia, outflow tract obstruction, and sudden death. Atomoxetine is the preferred non-stimulant first-line for adult ADHD in this scenario with a favourable cardiovascular risk profile. Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring is still needed as atomoxetine can raise both. Bupropion and modafinil are not first-line for ADHD in Australia.
key_points: Structural heart disease is a relative contraindication to stimulants for ADHD
Atomoxetine (selective NRI) is preferred non-stimulant first-line in this scenario
Atomoxetine still needs BP and HR monitoring
Bupropion and modafinil are not first-line for ADHD in Australia
explanation.pearls: In adult ADHD with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or a structural cardiac lesion, atomoxetine beats stimulants; the ICD does not make it safe to start a stimulant.

stem:
A 30-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis is admitted to your inpatient psychiatry unit. Over 48 hours he has become progressively withdrawn with reduced oral intake. On the morning of day 3 he is found lying on his bed, eyes open but unresponsive to verbal commands. He has not been on any regular medication. There is no history of head trauma or fever.

On examination he is mute, staring, and shows waxy flexibility (his arm remains in whatever position it is placed). He has echopraxia (mimicking the examiner's arm movements when tested) and marked negativism (resisting attempts at passive movement). Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no rigidity, no tremor, no autonomic instability, and no localising neurology. CT head is normal. Urinalysis is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Mute; staring; waxy flexibility; echopraxia; negativism; no rigidity; no tremor; no autonomic instability; no focal neurology; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L; CRP 4 mg/L; creatine kinase 92 U/L; sodium 140 potassium 4.0 creatinine 76; TSH 2.0 mIU/L; venous gas within normal limits; urinalysis clear; urine drug screen negative; CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral bromocriptine 2.5 milligrams three times daily as a dopamine agonist with concurrent intravenous dantrolene to reverse muscular rigidity
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS, not catatonia. This patient has no rigidity, autonomic instability, or raised CK; the picture is pure catatonia without NMS overlap. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

options.text: Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 milligrams to treat the underlying psychotic disorder and reassess catatonic features over the next 4 to 6 hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and increase the risk of NMS in a patient who is already catatonic. First-line is a lorazepam challenge, and antipsychotics are added only after catatonia is controlled. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

options.text: Commence intravenous acyclovir 10 milligrams per kilogram three times daily empirically for possible herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting cerebrospinal fluid PCR
options.rationale: There is no fever, altered vitals, focal neurology, or CSF or imaging evidence of encephalitis. Empirical aciclovir is not indicated in an afebrile patient with classic Bush-Francis catatonic signs. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

options.text: Refer for immediate bilateral electroconvulsive therapy as first-line treatment for suspected catatonia given the risk of malignant catatonia developing acutely
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is second-line in AU practice after a lorazepam challenge has been tried. It is escalated to when lorazepam is ineffective or in the presence of malignant catatonia (which requires autonomic instability, not present here). (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 milligrams as a challenge and observe over 20 to 30 minutes for improvement in mutism, negativism, and posturing
options.rationale: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale features (mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism) meet catatonia diagnostic criteria in DSM-5. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, observe for symptom improvement over 20-30 min) is the standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic step. Responders continue on regular lorazepam 6-24 mg/day. ECT is second-line if lorazepam fails. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: This is catatonia (Bush-Francis features: mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism) without autonomic instability or rigidity to suggest malignant catatonia. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, observed over 20-30 min) is both diagnostic and initial therapy; a positive response is dramatic. Responders continue on regular lorazepam 6-24 mg/day, tapered as symptoms resolve. ECT is second-line if lorazepam fails or if malignant catatonia develops (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity, raised CK). Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and NMS.
key_points: Bush-Francis features: mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism, posturing
First-line: lorazepam challenge 1-2 mg IV, observe 20-30 min
Second-line: ECT if lorazepam fails or malignant catatonia
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and NMS
explanation.pearls: Give 1-2 mg IV lorazepam as your first move in a new catatonia; do NOT reach for olanzapine, which can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS.
